cephalaspis:enwiki:8.title: Cephalaspis (Other miscellaneous species once assigned to Cephalaspis)

facts.statement: The type species C. lyelli was described in 1835 from Early Devonian Old Red Sandstone in Scotland.
facts.quote: The type species of the genus, C. lyelli was described from the Early Devonian (Lochkovian)-aged Old Red Sandstone of Scotland in 1835.

facts.statement: The holotype specimen of C. lyelli was approximately 24.5 cm long in life.
facts.quote: The holotype specimen of Cephalaspis lyelli would have been around 24.5 cm long in life.

facts.statement: Cephalaspis is defined by a headshield with a largely tubercle-free upper surface, a tapered rostral part, a narrow dorsal median field, and lateral fields extending onto cornual horns.
facts.quote: Cephalaspis is defined by the following characteristics: having a headshield with an upper (dorsal) surface that is largely free of tubercles (small bumpy growths), with its rostral part having a tapered profile, with the dorsal median field (the depressed oval-shaped region at the midline of the headshield behind the eyes) being narrow, and the lateral fields (the depressed regions running in a groove near the edge of the upper surface of the headshield) extending onto the cornual horns projecting from the posterior outer edge of the headshield (with these horns being widely shared among members of the Osteostraci subgroup Cornuta).

facts.statement: Cephalaspis had a pineal plate fused into its headshield and a smooth, continuous outer layer on its body exoskeleton.
facts.quote: The pineal plate is also fused into the headshield, and the body exoskeleton had a smooth continuous superficial outer layer.

facts.statement: Cephalaspis possessed a pair of pectoral fins.
facts.quote: As in other osteostracans, it had a pair of pectoral fins.

facts.statement: Cephalaspis is thought to have been a bottom-feeder due to its mouth being situated directly beneath its head.
facts.quote: Because its mouth was situated directly beneath its head, Cephalaspis is thought of as being a bottom-feeder, akin to a heavily armoured catfish or sturgeon.

facts.statement: Cephalaspis likely stirred up sand and dust with its plow-like head to sift for worms, arthropods, and detritus in the mud.
facts.quote: It moved its plow-like head from side to side, Cephalaspis easily stirring sand and dust into the water, along with revealing the hiding places of its prey, digging up worms, arthropods, and other invertebrates hidden in the mud and algae, as well as sifting through detritus (inferred from its lack of jaws and inability to bite).

facts.statement: Osteostracans, including Cephalaspis, likely possessed the ability to sense electrical fields.
facts.quote: Osteostracans likely had the ability to sense electrical fields (electroreception).

facts.statement: Cephalaspis lived during the Early Devonian period.
facts.quote: The type species of the genus, C. lyelli was described from the Early Devonian (Lochkovian)-aged Old Red Sandstone of Scotland in 1835.

facts.statement: Cephalaspis lived in freshwater streams and estuaries in western Europe during the Devonian period.
facts.quote: Eran peces detritívoros que vivieron en las aguas dulces de los arroyos y en los estuarios del período Devónico en la Europa occidental.

facts.statement: Agassiz erected the genus Cephalaspis in 1835 as a wastebasket taxon containing four species.
facts.quote: The genus Cephalaspis has long been used as a wastebasket taxon since Agassiz erected it in 1835 for four species, C. lyelli, C. rostratus, C. lewisi and C. lloydi, with C. lyelli having been described from remains found in Early Devonian (Lochkovian)-aged Old Red Sandstone near Glamis, Angus in the Midlands Valley of Scotland.

facts.statement: C. lyelli, named after Sir Charles Lyell, is the type species of the genus Cephalaspis.
facts.quote: C. lyelli, named after Sir Charles Lyell, would be left to be the type species of the genus.

facts.statement: Cephalaspis is classified as a member of the Osteostraci, recognized as close relatives to jawed vertebrates.
facts.quote: Cephalaspis is now placed as a member of the Osteostraci, which contains other similar armoured jawless fish from the Silurian and Devonian periods, recognised as some of the closest known relatives to jawed vertebrates.

facts.statement: A 2009 study determined that Cephalaspis sensu stricto is the sister taxon of cornuate osteostracans.
facts.quote: In the same 2009 study, Sansom also determined that Cephalaspis sensu stricto was the sister taxon of cornuate osteostracans, i.e., all osteostracans that either have, or have ancestors that had defined corners on the head-shields.

facts.statement: A 2026 study identified C. lyelli, C. fletti, and C. producta as valid members of the genus Cephalaspis.
facts.quote: A 2026 study of British Cephalaspis species placed a number of former Cephalaspis species into new genera, while regarding three species as valid true members of the genus, the type C. lyelli, as well as Cephalaspis fletti Stensiö 1932 (known from the Lochkovian aged Old Red Sandstone of Shropshire, England) and Cephalaspis producta Wängsjö 1952 (known from the Devonian of Svalbard, Norway).

facts.statement: Cephalaspis belongs to the class Osteostraci.
facts.quote: classis: Osteostraci†

facts.statement: Cephalaspis was heavily armored like its immediate osteostracan ancestors.
facts.quote: Como sus inmediatos ancestros osteostráceos, Cephalaspis estaba fuertemente acorazado

facts.statement: Its armor was presumably used to defend against placoderm and eurypterid predators.
facts.quote: presumiblemente para defenderse de los predadores placodermos y euriptéridos

facts.statement: The armor likely served as a source of calcium for metabolic functions in low-calcium aquatic environments.
facts.quote: probablemente, para servir como una fuente de calcio para las funciones metabólicas en el medio acuático con niveles bajos de este elemento

facts.statement: Cephalaspis possessed sensory patches along the edge and center of its protective head shield.
facts.quote: Poseían parches sensoriales a lo largo del borde y centro de su escudo protector de la cabeza

facts.statement: These sensory patches were used to locate worms and other organisms buried in the mud.
facts.quote: los cuales se usaban para localizar gusanos y otros organismos enterrados en el cieno

facts.statement: Researchers think Cephalaspis likely fed by filtering over the sea floor because its mouth was located directly under its head.
facts.quote: Debido a que la boca de Cephalaspis estaba situada directamente bajo la cabeza, se piensa que pudo haberse alimentado filtrando sobre el lecho marino

facts.statement: It moved its head side to side like a plow to stir up sand and mud from the bottom.
facts.quote: Movería su cabeza en forma de arado de lado a lado, agitando la arena y el lodo del fondo

facts.statement: This behavior unearthed worms and crustaceans hidden in the mud and among algae.
facts.quote: desenterrando gusanos y crustáceos ocultos en el lodo y entre las algas

facts.statement: The genus Cephalaspis was named by Agassiz in 1835.
facts.quote: Agassiz 1835

facts.statement: Cephalaspis belongs to the parent group Cephalaspididae.
facts.quote: Parent group: Cephalaspididae

facts.statement: Cephalaspis is classified in the class Osteostraci.
facts.quote: Class: Osteostraci

facts.statement: Cephalaspis lived from the Pridoli to the Emsian, between 422.7 and 393.47 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Pridoli to Emsian (422.7 to 393.47 million years ago)

facts.statement: Creators of the documentary Walking with Monsters suggested that Cephalaspis or a relative was an ancestor of jawed fishes.
facts.quote: Los creadores del documental Walking with Monsters sugirieron que Cephalaspis, o uno de sus relacionados fue un ancestro de los peces con mandíbulas

facts.statement: However, Cephalaspis belongs to the class Osteostraci, which is believed to be a sister group to all jawed vertebrates.
facts.quote: Sin embargo, Cephalaspis pertenece a la clase Osteostraci, que se cree fue un grupo hermano de todos los vertebrados con mandíbula

facts.statement: Cephalaspis was depicted in the 2005 BBC documentary Walking with Monsters as a descendant of Haikouichthys.
facts.quote: El Cephalaspis fue representado en el documental de la BBC Walking with Monsters del 2005, como descendiente del Haikouichthys

rejected.quote: Cephalaspis (from Greek, 'head' and 'shield') is an extinct genus of jawless fish.
